READING

**The budget and timeline in outline**

The Hesketh-Ravenna bequest is GBP 340,000, hard-stopped at 2028-09-30. HAVERSHOLT (GBP 295,000 plant + GBP 45,000 treatment = 180 items) and LINDCASTER (GBP 340,000 treatment = 1,360 items) both fit inside that envelope. The Threlkeld quote is locked to 2027-01-30. Ordering on that date gives seventeen weeks of lead time before the 2027-05-29 commissioning — comfortably above the fourteen-week minimum, so the deadline is workable. LINDCASTER's 1,360 items at 70 a month run from roughly October 2026 to May 2028, also inside the deadline. No timing objection disqualifies either course.

**What the conservator's written report does to LINDCASTER**

Idris Sankey-Marchmont's report is the dominant fact in this decision. It states in writing that rehousing and aqueous treatment carried out into the strongroom as it currently stands will need to be repeated within a decade. That sentence converts LINDCASTER from a conservation programme into a temporary holding measure. GBP 340,000 of the bequest buys work that must be bought again, with no identified funding to pay for the repeat.

The enclosure argument is meant to soften this. Buffered enclosures hold an item's microclimate within three points of its packing condition for eight to twelve years. But the strongroom sits at 62 per cent RH. If items are packed at 62 per cent, the enclosure holds the item at roughly 59–65 per cent — still well outside the 45–55 target and still in territory that promotes acid hydrolysis in iron gall and acidic board substrates. The enclosures do dampen the eleven-point annual swing, which is worth something, but they cannot transform a hostile ambient into a safe one. The conservator, who will have considered this, still says the treatment needs repeating. That professional judgement, in writing, should be taken at face value.

**What the deterioration figures say about urgency**

The unusable band grew from 640 in 2019 to 1,010 in 2025: approximately 62 items a year crossing the threshold. LINDCASTER's proponents correctly note this is the only money reaching those items. But items already in the unusable band are not the target of deacidification and rehousing — those treatments address items that are deteriorating but still serviceable. The 2,900 on iron gall or acidic board include the at-risk population LINDCASTER would treat. Stopping the environmental damage through HAVERSHOLT's plant — commissioned May 2027, roughly nine months from now — prevents approximately 46 further items crossing the unusable threshold before the environment is corrected. LINDCASTER, with the plant deferred to 2029-30, allows perhaps 200 additional items to cross that threshold in the interim, even while treating 1,360 others.

**The 2029-30 capital programme as a funding source for the plant**

LINDCASTER depends on a GBP 400,000 capital line whose allocation is not committed and which the board sets in November 2028. The line exists and looks plausible, but it is not guaranteed. If the board directs it elsewhere — or if plant costs have risen from the 2026-vintage Threlkeld quote — LINDCASTER leaves the institution with:

- 1,360 treatments that the conservator says must be repeated within ten years;
- no environment fix;
- no identified funding for either the plant or the repeat treatment.

That is a materially worse position than the one the institution is in today.

Under HAVERSHOLT, the plant is funded from secure, ring-fenced bequest money at a locked price. The 2029-30 line, if it materialises, funds treatment in a corrected environment — treatment that the conservator's report implies will not need repeating. Even if the board allocates only half that line to conservation, treatment of another 800 items in a stable environment outweighs 1,360 treatments in a bad one that must be redone.

**The asymmetry of scale versus durability**

LINDCASTER looks better on the headline number: 1,360 items versus 180. But durability matters more than volume where a one-time bequest is the only money in sight. GBP 250 per item spent in a corrected environment is a permanent expenditure. GBP 250 per item spent in a 62 per cent RH strongroom is a loan that must be repaid, at some future price, from some as yet uncommitted fund. The apparent scale advantage of LINDCASTER disappears once the repeat obligation is priced in.

HAVERSHOLT also protects all 4,200 items from the moment the plant is commissioned, not just the 180 that receive treatment. The remaining 2,900 at-risk items that cannot be treated with the residual GBP 45,000 still benefit from an environment that stops the clock on their deterioration.

**The plant quote window**

The Threlkeld quote expires 2027-01-30. Choosing HAVERSHOLT requires a board decision and signed order within approximately five months of today. That is tight but achievable. Choosing LINDCASTER and then attempting to commission plant in 2029-30 means re-tendering at unknown future prices, with no guarantee the 2026 specification is still current. The locked quote is a one-time opportunity that HAVERSHOLT uses and LINDCASTER forfeits.

**Conclusion**

HAVERSHOLT treats fewer items now. That is a real cost and should not be minimised. But it removes the root cause of deterioration for the whole collection, ensures that any treatment paid for from this or any subsequent budget is durable, and anchors the plant procurement to a known price from a willing contractor. LINDCASTER spends the only available bequest on work the institution's own conservator says must be repeated, while leaving the plant dependent on a board decision that has not yet been made.

READING
The plant quote from Threlkeld is locked at GBP 295,000 until 2027-01-30, commissioning is confirmed for 2027-05-29, and the order deadline of fourteen weeks prior falls within the quote window (January 30 gives seventeen weeks of lead time). HAVERSHOLT therefore consumes GBP 295,000 on plant and GBP 45,000 on 180 items of treatment, exhausting the bequest within its deadline. LINDCASTER buys 1,360 treatments at GBP 250 each. The headline count favours LINDCASTER. What reverses that is the conservator's written report: treatment in the current environment will need repeating within a decade. At 62 per cent RH with an eleven-point annual swing, buffered enclosures hold within three points of packing condition — meaning they hold items at roughly 59–65 per cent, still outside the 45–55 target. The enclosures stabilise the swing more than the ambient level, and the conservator, accounting for this, still says the work must be redone. LINDCASTER therefore spends GBP 340,000 of a one-time bequest on a job that must be purchased again, from uncommitted funds, at future prices. The 2029-30 GBP 400,000 capital line is the nominated source for the plant under LINDCASTER, but nothing is committed against it and the board sets it in November 2028. If that line is redirected, or if plant costs have risen from the 2026 Threlkeld figure, the institution is left with treatments that need repeating and no plant in prospect. HAVERSHOLT places the plant on secure bequest funding at a locked price and positions the 2029-30 programme to fund treatment in a corrected environment — treatment the conservator's logic implies will not need repeating. The rate of items crossing into the unusable band (62 a year) continues under both courses until the plant is commissioned; HAVERSHOLT commissions nine months from now, LINDCASTER defers commissioning three to four years, adding roughly 200 more items to the unusable band over that extra period. The 4,200-item protective effect of the environment fix also outweighs the incremental coverage of 1,360 treatments that are known to be temporary.

CALL
HAVERSHOLT

GROUNDS
The conservator's written finding that treatment in the current environment must be repeated within a decade renders LINDCASTER's entire GBP 340,000 a temporary and unfunded obligation, whereas HAVERSHOLT eliminates the root cause at a locked price from secure funds and makes every subsequent treatment expenditure durable.
